s: A company routes all east-west traffic between spoke VPCs through a centralized inspection VPC that is attached to a transit gateway. AWS Network Firewall endpoints are deployed in two Availability Zones in the inspection VPC, and each transit gateway subnet routes to the firewall endpoint in its own Availability Zone. Stateless rules work as expected, but stateful rules intermittently drop return traffic for flows between workloads that run in different Availability Zones. Which change will resolve the issue with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Convert the stateful rules to stateless rules and add matching rules for the return traffic.
Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's transit gateway attachment so that both directions of each flow use the same Availability Zone and firewall endpoint.
Add a Network Firewall endpoint in a third Availability Zone and route each transit gateway subnet to the endpoints in the other Availability Zones.
Replace Network Firewall with third-party firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer in the inspection VPC, and leave the transit gateway attachment settings unchanged.

w.y: The drops are caused by asymmetric routing: the transit gateway can send each direction of a cross-AZ flow to a different AZ, so a different firewall endpoint sees the return traffic. Enabling appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment keeps both directions of a flow in the same AZ, a single setting with the LEAST operational overhead.

o.A: Hides the symptom by giving up stateful inspection and doubles rule maintenance.
o.B: Correct: appliance mode removes the asymmetric routing that breaks stateful inspection.
o.C: More endpoints and cross-AZ routing do not make flows symmetric and add data processing cost.
o.D: Large re-architecture, and without appliance mode the transit gateway still routes flows asymmetrically.
